column7: Shin-ei's historical account identifies the Honey Co. FY-6 Baby Crying Fuzz as released in 1967 and as the first incarnation of the later Super Fuzz family.
column10: Treat 1967 as the builder-reported family origin; exact first production quantity and every early enclosure variant remain separate questions.

column7: Shin-ei states that it branded the FY-6 in 1968 after the 1967 Honey Baby Crying version, creating the next clearly named state in the Super Fuzz family.
column10: Preserve Honey and Shin-ei as distinct branded production states within the same family.

column7: The Companion FY-2 is a separate Shin-ei product family from FY-6 and became another major Japanese fuzz identity sold in North America.
column10: Do not merge FY-2 with FY-6 merely because both are associated with Shin-ei.

column7: Companion-branded FY-6 examples belong to the Super Fuzz family and represent a distinct retail-brand state after the earlier Honey and Shin-ei labels.
column10: Exact first Companion-branded production date remains subject to catalog and specimen reconciliation.

column7: Early Univox Super-Fuzz examples used a simple stamped steel enclosure with a blue metal badge before the later die-cast format became dominant.
column10: External enclosure construction is a high-value specimen clue; avoid assigning an exact cutoff without dated examples.

column7: Later U-1095 Super-Fuzz production shifted to the familiar die-cast enclosure, with multiple documented exterior color combinations.
column10: Treat paint/color variants as specimen evidence rather than separate families unless independent product documentation requires it.

column7: The U-250 Uni-Fuzz is a distinct Univox fuzz model associated with the broader Japanese/Shin-ei ecosystem and should not be collapsed into U-1095.
column10: Preserve U-250 as its own model record even when family lineage is shared or adjacent.

column7: Teisco Wau Wau Fuzz belongs to a Japanese OEM fuzz-wah family that appears under multiple regional brand identities.
column10: Model-level identification should emphasize enclosure, control arrangement and branding relationships.

column7: Ace Tone's FM-1 predates the FM-2 and belongs to the earliest Ace Tone Fuzz Master sequence.
column10: Use a broad late-1960s window until period catalog evidence establishes a tighter start date.

column7: Period advertising and catalog research place the FM-2 in market by March 1968 and show the model continuing through Ace Tone catalogs into the 1970s.
column10: March 1968 is an unusually strong period-document anchor and should supersede older generic 1969-71 estimates.

column7: Ace Tone introduced FM-3 as a later Fuzz Master model distinct from FM-1 and FM-2, appearing in the 1970s product sequence.
column10: Keep FM-3 separate from the earlier Super Fuzz-copy lineage assumptions around FM-2.

column7: Guyatone's 1969 catalog introduced the FS-2 Buzz Box, providing a dated anchor immediately before the later FS-3 fuzz.
column10: Use 1969 as the catalog anchor for FS-2; exact first-sale month is not established here.

column7: Later Guyatone catalogs show FS-3 between the FS-2 Buzz Box and FS-5/FS-6 products, with current research placing its release after 1970 and by 1972.
column10: Prefer the broader release window over older unsupported single-year claims.

column7: A 1972-1973 Guyatone catalog shows the FS-5 Wah-Fuzz alongside the FS-3 Fuzz and FS-4 Wah-Wah.
column10: Catalog co-occurrence is useful chronology evidence; retain as a separate model from FS-3.

column7: Guyatone's FS-6 follows the earlier FS-series fuzz models as the later Fuzz Sustainer entry in the lineup.
column10: Keep the model identity separate even when its family role overlaps the earlier FS fuzz products.

column10: Model the Italian branch separately from British Sola Sound production while preserving the retail/OEM relationships.

column7: The Unicord Fuzz is documented as an Italian JEN-made fuzz related to the Vox Tone Bender V828/V8281 branch and sold for the North American market.
column10: Treat Unicord as a branded retail object within the Italian OEM network rather than a standalone unrelated design.

column7: Vox V828 belongs to the Italian JEN-associated Tone Bender branch and must remain distinct from the British Sola Sound MKII family.
column10: Country-of-production transitions and first Italian batch dates require further primary catalog reconciliation.
